First edition · 2017 · O'Reilly Media

The Manager's Path

Camille Fournier

The Manager's Path: A Guide for Tech Leaders Navigating Growth and Change follows the career of an engineering manager level by level, from being managed to running a technology organization. Each chapter covers one step up in management complexity — mentor, tech lead, manager of people, of a team, of multiple teams, of managers, and senior leadership — so readers can start at the chapter that matches their job and come back as it changes (Introduction, pp. xi–xiv). Chapter 9, on culture, is the "wildcard" that applies at every level.

Recurring boxes give the book its texture: Ask the CTO answers common questions, Good Manager, Bad Manager contrasts behaviours (the alpha geek, the process czar, the micromanager), and Challenging Situations walks through hard conversations. Each chapter ends with questions for Assessing Your Own Experience. The author began the book while CTO at Rent the Runway, and its examples come from there and from her earlier jobs.

How the book fits together

The chapters climb the management ladder; the last two step back to culture and to managing yourself.

The ladder order is the book's; the dotted links are the vault's reading of where Chapter 9 applies.

Some threads run through the whole book:

  • 1-1s and feedback start as something you receive (1), become your main tool with people (4), and turn into skip-levels as you move away from the work (7).
  • Staying technical shifts from writing code (3, 5) to code reviews and debugging (6) to setting technical standards and True North (8).
  • Delegation grows from the tech lead's balance (3) through the delegation table (6) to managing managers you can't micromanage (7).
  • Culture and fear: the alpha geek's culture of fear (2), team culture (5, 6), the senior leader's influence (8), and deliberate culture-building (9).

Simulations

Interactive models of the mechanisms the book describes. They are embedded in the lessons too; implementations are the vault’s own.

  • Chapter 2Sizing an intern projectSet the internship length, the intern's pace and the program's other activities, and see whether a project sized at half the internship gets finished.
  • Chapter 3Maker’s schedule, manager’s schedulePlace meetings on a week's calendar and watch how many uninterrupted coding blocks survive when the same meetings are scattered or batched.
  • Chapter 4Whole year or last two months?A year of observed work, scored once from memory that favours recent months and once from running 1-1 notes, to see how recency changes a review.
  • Chapter 5Quarter capacity plannerSize a team, pick a quarter, set the sustaining share, and see which projects fit once estimates are doubled and the 10-week rule applies.
  • Chapter 6Delegate or do it yourself?Sort the book's own example tasks into Table 6-1's urgency/importance quadrants and Table 6-2's complexity/frequency quadrants, and see what each placement tells you to do.
  • Chapter 8Which senior role is this?Tick the building blocks a senior technology job involves and see which of the book's combinations and titles match.
  • Chapter 9Levels and salary bandsChoose few wide overlapping levels or many narrow ones, starting from the book's example bands, and see how promotion pace, overlap and pay spread change.

Key concepts

These ideas recur across chapters; each row lists the chapters that discuss them. The definitions are the vault's summaries of the book's explanations.

ConceptDefinitionChapters
1-1 meetingsRegular private meetings between manager and report: for human connection, feedback and coaching, not status updates.1 · 4 · 7
Continuous feedbackSmall, frequent praise and correction, so reviews hold no surprises.1 · 4
Alpha geekThe engineer who must be the smartest in the room; creates a culture of fear, not excellence.2 · 8
Tech leadA set of responsibilities, not a level: balancing your own technical work with what the team needs.3 · 9
Process czarThe lead who believes the right process will solve every problem; the alternative is process fitted to the team.3 · 9
MicromanagementControlling the details of delegated work; the delegator instead sets goals and checks in at the right depth.4 · 6 · 7
Sustaining engineeringAbout 20% of planned time reserved for testing, cleanup, migrations and on-call, so features don't slow down.5 · 9
Importance vs. urgencyTable 6-1: urgency is felt, importance must be judged; make time for the important but not urgent.6
Delegation by complexity and frequencyTable 6-2: delegate simple frequent work, do simple rare work, teach complex work to grow the team.6 · 7
Skip-level meetingsMeetings with your reports' reports — quarterly 1-1s or team lunches — to see past managers who manage up well.7
First teamA leader's first team is their peers across the company, not the people who report to them.6 · 8
True NorthThe standards a senior leader sets — such as production readiness — that teams internalize and weigh risks against.8
Career ladderLevels with written expectations and salary bands, written with the team and evolved as it grows.8 · 9
Process as risk managementHeavy process only for rare or hidden-risk work; code review, blameless postmortems and architecture review depersonalize decisions.9
